intro: Drnava is a small village in eastern Slovakia, nicknamed Kis Pest, Little Pest, after a 19th-century ironworks that cast structural parts for Budapest's Chain Bridge. Its oak has outlasted the works by centuries: about 700 years old, recorded in the village chronicle since 1670, and named Slovakia's tree of the year in 2020 after taking 5,246 of nearly 25,000 votes cast.
meta_description: Drnava's oak, about 700 years old and recorded since 1670, won Slovakia's Tree of the Year 2020 with over 5,000 votes. Free village trail, no ticket.
question_meta: Drnava's oldest tree is its 700-year-old oak, in the village chronicle since 1670 and Slovakia's Tree of the Year 2020.
question_answer:
The oldest tree in Drnava is the pedunculate oak standing at stop two of the village's own Poklady Drnavy nature trail, reckoned at about 700 years old. It appears in the village chronicle from 1670, which means it was already old when anyone here first wrote it down.

In 2020 it took 5,246 of the 24,839 votes cast in Strom roka, Slovakia's national tree of the year contest, and went on to represent the country at the European Tree of the Year. It is not a tall tree, 14 metres, but its trunk runs 528 centimetres round with a crown spreading 21 metres, the shape ancient oaks take once they stop reaching up and start reaching sideways.
question_context:
The oak stands on open ground within the built-up village, free, with nothing to book, on the Poklady Drnavy (Treasures of Drnava) educational trail. The nearest railway station is Roznava, followed by a regional bus to Drnava, and there is no direct rail link into the village itself.

The ground around the tree has its own history worth knowing before you go. Drnava was nicknamed Kis Pest, Little Pest, after the Andrassy ironworks that operated here in the nineteenth century and cast structural parts for the Chain Bridge in Budapest in the 1840s. The oak had already stood in the village chronicle for 170 years by the time that works was built, and it grows near the former site today, one stop among several on the village's own trail.

The trail itself is a short, signed walk rather than a demanding hike, and the oak is the obvious highlight of it: a broad, low crown rather than a tall one, easy to recognise from a distance once you know what an oak this old actually looks like. Nothing here needs a ticket, a guide or advance planning; it rewards simply turning up.
